title: Fundamental Data Types and Type Sizes
learningObjectives: Explain the central rules behind fundamental data types and type sizes in C.
Identify the relevant types, declarations, operators or library facilities.
Trace a worked example and explain its result.
Recognize common mistakes, portability concerns and unsafe assumptions.
Apply the concept in a small program and test normal and boundary cases.

understand.concept: C provides character types, signed and unsigned integer types, and floating types. The exact width of several types is implementation-defined, subject to minimum range requirements. sizeof reports an object's or type's size in bytes for the current implementation; a byte is CHAR_BIT bits and is not guaranteed to be eight bits on every conforming implementation.
understand.whyItMatters: Portable code must not assume that int is always 32 bits or that long has the same width on every platform. Use the language guarantees, sizeof, limits headers and fixed-width types when an exact width is required.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
C provides character types, signed and unsigned integer types, and floating types. The exact width of several types is implementation-defined, subject to minimum range requirements. sizeof reports an object's or type's size in bytes for the current implementation; a byte is CHAR_BIT bits and is not guaranteed to be eight bits on every conforming implementation.

Portable code must not assume that int is always 32 bits or that long has the same width on every platform. Use the language guarantees, sizeof, limits headers and fixed-width types when an exact width is required.

When reviewing code, identify the declared types first, then trace conversions and the exact expression being evaluated. Compile with warnings enabled and test boundary values. Do not rely on assumptions about another compiler or machine.

examples.title: Core example
examples.code: printf("char=%zu int=%zu long=%zu double=%zu\\n", sizeof(char), sizeof(int), sizeof(long), sizeof(double));
examples.explanation: sizeof produces a size_t result. The output reports sizes for the compiler and target used; it is not a universal table.

examples.title: A second case
examples.explanation: The limits macros describe the range of the corresponding integer type on the current implementation.

practise.guidedTask: Compile a program that reports sizeof for the fundamental types and prints integer limits from limits.h. Record the compiler and target.
practise.independentTask: Compare the output on two compiler targets if available. Explain which results are guaranteed by the C standard and which are implementation-dependent.
hints: sizeof reports a size in bytes, not a universal bit width.
Use limits.h macros to inspect integer ranges.
Do not assume int is always 32 bits.
Use fixed-width types from stdint.h when exact widths are required and available.

questions.prompt: What is the safest general practice?
options: Choose types and operations deliberately, initialize data and validate assumptions.
Ignore warnings and assume values are valid.
Use casts to silence every warning.
questions.answer: Choose types and operations deliberately, initialize data and validate assumptions.
questions.explanation: Deliberate types and checks improve correctness.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a result is unexpected?
options: Create a small test case and inspect types, values and conversions.
Guess the result from the variable name.
questions.answer: Create a small test case and inspect types, values and conversions.
questions.explanation: Small reproducible tests make behaviour easier to reason about.

questions.prompt: Which statement about portability is accurate?
options: Some type sizes and ranges depend on the implementation.
All C implementations use identical type widths.
Compiler warnings change the C standard.
questions.answer: Some type sizes and ranges depend on the implementation.
questions.explanation: Use standard guarantees and inspect implementation limits.
